summary: Put inputs on a similar scale and descent stops zig-zagging.
headline: Same data, different units, very different speed
overview: When one input is measured in the hundreds and another is between 0 and 1, the loss bowl becomes a long narrow ravine. A learning rate safe for the steep side is tiny for the flat side.
Standardising each input to zero mean and unit spread makes the bowl round.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Leave the features raw. Even at the fastest safe learning rate, the loss crawls for hundreds of steps.

check.question: Closed-form least squares gives the same predictions with or without scaling. Why scale anyway?
options: It changes the answer a lot
Gradient descent and penalties behave better

realLife: Models with a penalty, distance-based models and neural networks all need it. Tree models do not.
data: Thirty rows. Feature one is 0 to 1, feature two is 0 to 300. The target depends on both. Both runs use 90% of their own stable learning-rate limit.
maths: scikit-learn's StandardScaler divides by the population std (n, not n−1).
Fit the scaler on training data only, then reuse its mean and std on new data.
code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge()).fit(X_train, y_train)
